outline.description: Sets the stage by outlining the parties, the patents at issue, the lower‑court trial, and the appellate posture. This chapter provides the factual context needed to understand the technical disputes and explains the procedural steps that led to the Federal Circuit review.
subtopics: The patents: U.S. Pat. Nos. 7,346,134 and 9,548,775 – technical field and inventorship
Finesse Wireless LLC as patent holder; AT&T Mobility and Nokia as alleged infringers
Key technical concepts: intermodulation products (IMP), passive intermodulation (PIM), and PIM cancellation (PIM‑C)
Trial court proceedings: jury verdict on infringement and damages, motions for JMOL and new trial
Appeal jurisdiction and issues presented on appeal

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Legal Framework for JMOL and Claim Construction
outline.description: Explains the standards governing judgment‑as‑a‑matter‑of‑law (JMOL) motions, the de novo review of claim constructions, and the burden of proof in infringement cases. It also clarifies the Fifth Circuit’s approach, which the Federal Circuit applied on appeal.
subtopics: JMOL standard: de novo review of the evidence and “substantial evidence” test for jury findings
Burden of proof for infringement – plaintiff’s responsibility to prove each claim limitation
Claim construction principles: Markman de novo review, role of intrinsic and extrinsic evidence, “clear and unambiguous” disavowal doctrine
Fifth Circuit precedent on JMOL and claim construction reviewed by the Federal Circuit
Interaction between expert testimony and the court’s factual findings

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Infringement Analysis of the ’134 Patent
outline.description: Breaks down the Federal Circuit’s reasoning on the first patent, focusing on the contested limitation that the accused radios must sample both “signals of interest” and “interference‑generating signals.” The chapter evaluates the expert testimony, the court’s construction, and why the appellate court found the jury’s finding unsupported.
subtopics: Claim‑1 language of the ’134 patent – oversampling, isolation, estimation, and cancellation steps
Finesse’s burden: proof that the accused radios sample a passband containing both signal types
Expert Dr. Jonathan Wells’s testimony – mapping of DL(TX) reference and modeled PIM path to claim terms
Cross‑examination revelations: the modeled PIM path is generated downstream of the ADC and cannot be sampled
Court’s assessment of the contradictory and ambiguous testimony
Application of the “substantial evidence” standard – why the evidence did not meet the burden
Resulting reversal of the JMOL denial for the ’134 patent

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: Infringement Analysis of the ’775 Patent
outline.description: Analyzes the second patent, emphasizing the disputed “three signals S1, S2, S3” limitation and the requirement of seven third‑order multiplications. The chapter details the expert’s evidence, the claim construction, and the Federal Circuit’s conclusion that the jury’s verdict lacked evidentiary support.
subtopics: Claim‑1 language of the ’775 patent – generation of IMP cancellation signals using three signals and seven multiplications
Construction of “three separately identifiable signals” – intrinsic vs. extrinsic evidence
Finesse’s argument on claim scope and alleged surrender of two‑signal coverage
Expert testimony on the Nokia document – identification of three distinct multiplications only
Failure to show how three distinct multiplications map onto the seven claimed multiplications
Assessment of the plaintiff’s failure to present evidence of the required ten or seven multiplications
Application of the “substantial evidence” standard and reversal of the JMOL denial for the ’775 patent

outline.description: Discusses the district court’s denial of a new trial on damages, the Federal Circuit’s approach to reviewing that denial, and the ultimate vacatur of the $166 million award. The chapter also reflects on the broader implications for patent infringement litigation and expert testimony standards.
subtopics: District court’s post‑verdict motions: JMOL on damages and new‑trial request
Fifth Circuit/ Federal Circuit standard for reviewing denial of a new trial – abuse of discretion
Effect of reversing the JMOL denials on the damages award – vacatur and cost award
Policy considerations: holding parties to clear expert testimony, preventing speculative infringement findings
Implications for future PIM‑related patent cases and for claim‑scope amendments during prosecution
